identity.name: Tibetans (Era of Fragmentation)
alt_names: Tibet in the Era of Fragmentation

land.text: the empire's land at its end, without the Dzungaria and Turfan land the Uyghurs had taken

predecessors.note: Cliopatria's Tibetan Empire row runs to 849 and this row starts in 850; the break is moved to 842, Langdarma's assassination.

land.text: the Tibetan plateau, under Mongol overlordship from the late 1240s

successors.note: Sakya Pandita was appointed Viceroy of Central Tibet by the Mongol court in 1249 (History of Tibet page); Mongke's armies entered Tibet in 1252-1255, Phagpa became Imperial Preceptor in 1260 and Tibet was run by the Bureau of Buddhist and Tibetan Affairs under Kublai (Mongol conquest of Tibet page). Cliopatria's next Tibetan row, 'Tibet', begins in 1363 (another group).

correction.text: the Tibetan Empire's corrected 840 shape, held by the rival Tibetan lords

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe for 842-849, which Cliopatria gives to the Tibetan Empire's last shape (3.86 M km2). Langdarma 'was assassinated in 842 possibly by a Buddhist hermit' and 'the two princes Yumtan and Osung ... fought for the throne and initiated a civil war'; Dzungaria and the Turfan basin were already Uyghur (792). The corrected 840 shape (3.59 M km2) is drawn for 842-849 and the ledger takes Shazhou and Guazhou (848), the Hexi and Tarim (850) from it.

correction.text: the plateau plus Liangzhou (Wuwei), held by Tibetan generals until Zhang Yichao's authority reached it by 861

keyframe_review.note: 1.87 M km2 (the plateau alone). The Guiyi Circuit page has Tibetan generals Kongre and Bibi still in the Hexi in 850-851 and Guiyi authority reaching Liangzhou only 'by 861', so Liangzhou stays with the Tibetans for 850-860 (the Tibetan state of Xiliangfu is there by 906).

correction.text: the plateau plus Liangzhou until the 861 loss

keyframe_review.note: 1.87 M km2 (the plateau alone); Liangzhou goes to Guiyi in 861 ('By 861, Guiyi's authority covered ... Liangzhou, Lanzhou ...'), so the shape begins with Liangzhou and the ledger removes it.

1.87 M km2, the plateau; no page changes it. In 866 Zhang Yichao 'defeated the Tibetan general bLon Khrom brZhe (Kongre), seized Luntai (Urumqi) and Tingzhou' (Guiyi page), land outside the polygon. Stands.

1.87 M km2 for 875-959, the plateau. Kyide Nyimagon 'moved to Ngari in 910 ... established a kingdom around 912, annexing Purang and Guge' (Guge page; c. 900 on the Ladakh page), which takes Ngari out of any central polity; the polygon keeps Ngari inside until that kingdom has a dossier (counterparts list). Stands as the Tibetan lands.

1.85 M km2, the plateau. About 930 Nyimagon's lands were divided among three sons: Maryul (Ladakh), Rutog and Demchok, Guge-Purang, Zanskar and Spiti (Ladakh page); all inside the polygon, none drawn apart. Stands.
1.84 M km2, the plateau; Yeshe-O took vows in 988 and Atisa was invited 'in 1040' (Guge page, 1042 on History of Tibet). No border moves. Stands.

1.84 M km2, the plateau; the Sakya school was founded by Khon Konchok Gyelpo (1034-1102) and Rinchen Zangpo's temples date from the late 10th-11th centuries (History of Tibet page). No border moves. Stands.

1.86 M km2, the plateau; 'Between 842 and 1247, no central authority was in control of Tibet', with Guge, Derge, Nangchen and Maryul as the smaller kingdoms the page names. Stands as the Tibetan lands.
1.86 M km2, the plateau; Tsang-pa Dung-khur and six disciples met Genghis Khan in 1221-22, probably on the Tangut border. Stands.

1.86 M km2, the plateau, for 1241-1249: Doorda Darkhan's raid of 1240 burned Reting and Gyal Lha Khang and the Mongols withdrew in 1241; Sakya Pandita urged the Tibetan leaders to submit in the late 1240s. Stands to 1249.

correction.text: no Tibetan state in 1250-1259: the plateau of the 1249 shape is drawn as Mongol Empire land (a vassal tint in the Mongol dossier)

keyframe_review.note: Cliopatria's 1250-1259 shape is a 10-cell remnant (2,000 km2 near the Nepal border at 85.3-86.3 E), because its Mongol Empire shape takes the plateau in 1250. Sakya Pandita was appointed Viceroy of Central Tibet in 1249; the plateau itself is Mongol-overseen from then, not Tibetan-ruled, so this dossier ends in 1249.

region.text: the Tibetan Empire's land at its end

ledger.note: 842: Langdarma is assassinated and Tibet breaks into rival lords. He 'was assassinated in 842 possibly by a Buddhist hermit monk named Pelgyi Dorje of Lhalung'; his sons Yumtan and Osung 'fought for the throne and initiated a civil war' and 'between 842 and 1247, no central authority was in control of Tibet'. Osung's allies kept Lhasa, Yumtan went to Yalung (History of Tibet).
848: Zhang Yichao rises at Dunhuang. He 'led an uprising and captured Shazhou and Guazhou from the Tibetans'.

region.text: Ganzhou, Suzhou and Yizhou (the Hexi Corridor beyond Liangzhou and Dunhuang, and Hami)

ledger.note: 850: the Hexi is lost. 'By 850 Zhang had captured Ganzhou, Suzhou, and Yizhou' while the Tibetan generals Kongre and Bibi fought each other in the Hexi; Liangzhou stays Tibetan until 861. The page does not say whom Zhang took each city from.

region.text: the Tarim Basin, freed or taken by others by the mid-9th century

ledger.note: 850: the Tarim is gone. Page dating only by the mid-9th century: the Four Garrisons 'all eventually ended up freeing themselves or coming under the dominion of other powers'; Cliopatria's 850 shape drops the Tarim and the kingdom-of-khotan dossier has Khotan independent from 851. [Reviewer ea-04-b: confidence 2 -> 1; the page gives no year (mid-9th century), 850 is Cliopatria's step.]

region.text: Liangzhou and the Hexi prefectures that came under Guiyi

ledger.note: 861: Liangzhou goes. 'By 861, Guiyi's authority covered Guazhou, Ganzhou, Suzhou, Yizhou, Lanzhou, Shanzhou, Hezhou, Minzhou, Liangzhou, and Kuozhou'; Guiyi control slipped c. 881-882 and a Tibetan state, Xiliangfu, was at Liangzhou by 906.

region.text: the Tibetan plateau, under Mongol overlordship

ledger.note: 1249: Tibet passes under Mongol overlordship. 'Sakya Pandita was appointed Viceroy of Central Tibet by the Mongol court' in 1249 after urging the Tibetan leaders to submit; Mongke's armies entered in 1252-1255 and 'most of Tibet likely came under Mongol control afterward' (Mongol conquest of Tibet page). The Era of Fragmentation ended 'with the Mongol conquest of Tibet' (1247 on that page).

wars.name: Zhang Yichao's revolt
wars.outcome: Zhang took Shazhou and Guazhou in 848, Ganzhou, Suzhou and Yizhou by 850 and Xizhou in 851 while the Tibetan generals Kongre and Bibi fought each other (clashes in the eighth and ninth months of 850); the Tang named his land Guiyi Prefecture in 851.
wars.note: Kongre asked the Tang for a title in May 851, was refused and withdrew to Kuozhou with about 300 men.

wars.name: Tibetan civil war after Langdarma
belligerents: Yumtan and the lords of U
Osung and his allies at Lhasa
wars.outcome: Yumtan and Osung fought for the throne; Osung's allies held Lhasa, Yumtan went to Yalung. 'Between 842 and 1247, no central authority was in control of Tibet.' The page gives no end year, so the span is the one dated year.

wars.name: Mongol raid on Tibet

zones.text: Reting and Gyal Lha Khang, north-east of Lhasa

wars.outcome: Doorda Darkhan's 30,000 burned the Reting and Gyal Lha Khang monasteries in 1240 and withdrew in 1241, recalled by Ogedei's succession.

wars.name: Mongol conquest of Tibet
wars.outcome: Koten summoned the Sakya abbot in 1244; Sakya Pandita urged submission, met Koten at Lanzhou in 1247 and was made viceroy in 1249; several Mongol armies entered Tibet in 1252-1255 and most of it was probably under Mongol control afterwards. The page gives no battle.
wars.note: The pages differ on dates (see notes); no clear map of land held directly by the Mongols and by the Sakya exists on them.

certainty.note: No page gives a frontier for any Tibetan principality; the plateau polygon is Cliopatria's and the western, northern and eastern edges are approximate. The Hexi lines of 848-861 are city by city, not borders.

notes:
Written 2026-10-19 by the ea-04-b research agent from the Era of Fragmentation, History of Tibet, Guge and Mongol conquest of Tibet pages (the page budget is five; the Ladakh, Guiyi Circuit and Protectorate General to Pacify the West pages opened for tibetan-empire are also cited, so six pages are cited in all). The Wikipedia title Cliopatria gives, 'Tibetan people', was not opened: it is an ethnic article, not a history of a state.

What this row is. Cliopatria's 'Tibetans' (850..1259) is one polygon, the Tibetan plateau (4181 of 4342 cells of Xizang, 1805 of Qinghai's 2893, 1332 of Kham's 2243, 38 of Nepal's 580 and a fringe of the Kunlun), unchanged to within 0.1% in every shape from 850 to 1249. The pages open say the opposite of a state: 'Between 842 and 1247, no central authority was in control of Tibet' (Era of Fragmentation); 'The successors of Osung controlled the western region of Ngari', 'the successors of Yumtan ... the central region of U', and 'relatively smaller kingdoms like Guge, Derge, Nangchen, and Maryul (Ladakh) emerged'. The dossier keeps the polygon as the Tibetan lands in a time of fragmentation (type state for want of a better type; no capital is given because no seat is on the pages) and ends it in 1249, when the Mongol court appointed Sakya Pandita viceroy and Cliopatria hands the plateau to its Mongol Empire shape (a 10-cell remnant stays to 1259, verdict wrong).

Start and end. Cliopatria's Tibetan Empire row runs to 849 and this row starts in 850; the dossiers move the break to 842 (Langdarma's assassination), so tibetans_842 (new keyframe, 842-849) repeats the empire's corrected 840 shape, and the losses of 848 (Shazhou, Guazhou), 850 (Ganzhou, Suzhou, Yizhou, the Tarim) and 861 (Liangzhou) are events of this dossier. The Tarim's end is not dated by any page: the Protectorate page says only that the Four Garrisons 'all eventually ended up freeing themselves or coming under the dominion of other powers' by the mid-9th century; Kingdom of Khotan's dossier has 851.

Not modelled, because it needs its own dossier and a hole in this polygon: the kingdom of Kyide Nyimagon in Ngari ('moved to Ngari in 910 ... established a kingdom around 912, annexing Purang and Guge', Guge page; c. 900 on the Ladakh page), its division among three sons c. 930 (Maryul/Ladakh with Rutog and Demchok, Guge-Purang, Zanskar-Spiti), Guge's later history (Yeshe-O 988, Atisa 1040, Ladakhi siege 1630, Lhasa conquest 1679-80); and the Tibetan generals of the Hexi after 848: Kongre and Bibi (848-851), the Tibetan state of Xiliangfu at Liangzhou by 906 (Guiyi page). Other Tibetan-era facts on the pages that move no border: Atisa's invitation (1040 or 1042), the Sakya school (Khon Konchok Gyelpo 1034-1102), the Mongol raid of Doorda Darkhan in 1240 (burned Reting and Gyal Lha Khang, withdrew 1241), Sakya Pandita summoned in 1244 and meeting Koten in 1247, Phagpa 1253 and Imperial Preceptor 1260, the Anxi Prefecture of 1264, the 1268 census into thirteen myriarchies. The History of Tibet page says nothing of a Tsongkha or Amdo state; the Era of Fragmentation page says only that Amdo was 'conquered by a Tibetan polity in the 10th century'.

Disagreements: the Xizhou (Gaochang) entry in the tang-dynasty ledger (851, from 'tibetans') has no support here: the Uyghur page has the Uyghurs taking Gaochang from the Tibetans in 792 and the Guiyi page does not say whom Zhang Yichao took it from, so no 851 loss is recorded; the Guiyi page says Guiyi authority reached Liangzhou 'by 861' and slipped c. 881-882. Mongol dates differ between pages (1249 viceroy on History of Tibet, 1252-1255 armies on Mongol conquest of Tibet, 1253 Phagpa on both, 1264 vs 1260 for his preceptorship).

Counterparts without a dossier: Guiyi Circuit (848-1036), Guge/Ngari kingdom (c. 912-1630; suggested slug guge), Maryul / Ladakh (c. 930), Zanskar-Spiti, Xiliangfu (Liangzhou, by 906), Sakya (1073-). Family: 'india' as for the empire (no Tibetan family in colours.json).
